description: 100+ Top C++ LLD interview questions categorized by OOP, SOLID, Patterns, Concurrency, and Traps with interactive reveal.

topics.title: C++ OOP & Memory Interview Questions
topics.definition: High-yield interview questions probing object layout, virtual tables, dynamic casting, object slicing, RAII, and custom memory management in C++.
topics.why_it_matters: These technical questions test whether you understand what the C++ compiler actually produces at the assembly and memory level, separating senior engineers from casual programmers.
topics.real_world_analogy: A mechanic who doesn't just know how to drive a sports car, but understands internal combustion, transmission ratios, and ECU timing maps.
conceptual_breakdown: VTable & VPTR: 8-byte pointer per polymorphic object pointing to class function table.
Virtual Destructor: Required in any base class with virtual methods to prevent partial destructor deletion leaks.
Object Slicing: Passing derived objects by value cuts off derived members.
Rule of 0 / 3 / 5: Deterministic resource lifecycle management.

steps.description: CPU dereferences object's hidden `vptr` at offset 0.
Indexes slot 0 in `Circle_VTable` and jumps to `Circle::draw()` assembly.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Virtual Destructor Dispatch: Because ~Base() is virtual, deleting via Base* looks up Derived::~Derived() in the VTable, freeing heapBuffer.
2. Memory Leak Prevention: Without virtual ~Base(), only Base::~Base() executes, leaking the 100 ints.
3. Modern RAII: Wrapping with std::unique_ptr ensures deletion happens automatically when going out of scope.

comparison_matrix.title: C++ Casting Mechanisms
rows: Raw hardware buffers, packet byte serialization

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling virtual methods inside constructors or destructors
common_mistakes.correction: During base construction, the derived portion is not yet initialized; virtual calls resolve to the base class implementation, NOT the derived one.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why does `sizeof(EmptyClass)` return 1 byte in C++ instead of 0?'
Answer: C++ requires every distinct object instance to have a unique memory address (`&a != &b`). In C++20, `[[no_unique_address]]` allows empty members to consume 0 bytes.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Fix a missing virtual destructor in a polymorphic abstract base class.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: class Shape { public: virtual void draw() = 0; };
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: class Shape { public: virtual ~Shape() = default; virtual void draw() = 0; };

practice_problem.title: Analyze Virtual Table Sizing
practice_problem.description: Calculate the exact memory footprint of a class with 2 virtual functions, 1 int member, and 1 double member on a 64-bit architecture.

topics.title: SOLID Principles Interview Questions
topics.definition: Curated questions and deep technical trade-off scenarios on Single Responsibility, Open-Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion in C++.
topics.why_it_matters: Interviewers frequently present subtly flawed code snippets and ask candidates to identify which SOLID principle is violated and write the refactored C++ code.
topics.real_world_analogy: Building a modular modular stereo system: speakers, turntable, and amplifiers connect via standard RCA cables (DIP), allowing upgrading the turntable without rewiring the speakers (OCP).
conceptual_breakdown: SRP: A class should have only one reason to change.
OCP: Open for extension, closed for modification (via interfaces/templates).
LSP: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness.
ISP: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
DIP: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

steps.description: Function testRectangle(Rectangle& r) assumes setWidth(5) and setHeight(4) gives area 20.
Pass Square instance. setHeight(4) overrides width to 4. Area is 16 != 20! Invariant broken.
Refactor: Make Shape base with getArea(); separate Square and Rectangle hierarchies.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Preserving Invariants: Square is NOT a behavioral subtype of Rectangle if mutators (setWidth) allow altering independent dimensions.
2. Common Abstract Root: Both implement IShape with read-only contract getArea().
3. Immutability Principle: Making shapes immutable value objects completely eliminates LSP mutation bugs.

comparison_matrix.title: SOLID Principles Summary
rows: Does this class do 2 unrelated things?
Must I edit this file to add a new payment type?
Does class implement dummy no-op methods?
Split giant interface into smaller role interfaces
Does high-level service call concrete MySQL?

common_mistakes.mistake: Creating a single God Interface `IEntity` with 50 methods
common_mistakes.correction: Apply Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) to split into small interfaces (`IPrintable`, `ISerializable`, `IComparable`).

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Is Dependency Inversion Principle the same as Dependency Injection?'
Answer: No. DIP is the high-level design principle (depend on abstractions). Dependency Injection (DI) is a specific design pattern / technique used to deliver dependencies to a class (e.g. constructor injection).

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a NotificationService that directly instantiates SendGridAPI inside its constructor.

practice_problem.title: Identify SOLID Violations in Monolithic E-Commerce Cart
practice_problem.description: Given a `ShoppingCart` class that calculates taxes, charges Stripe, updates MySQL, and sends emails, refactor it into 4 SRP-compliant components.

topics.title: Design Patterns & Trade-offs Questions
topics.definition: Deep-dive questions comparing creational, structural, and behavioral patterns: Factory vs Abstract Factory, Strategy vs State, Observer vs Pub/Sub, and Decorator vs Adapter.
topics.why_it_matters: Interviewers test whether you understand the exact trade-offs of patterns rather than blindly applying them everywhere (Pattern Overuse / Anti-pattern).
topics.real_world_analogy: Choosing the right tool from a master mechanic's toolbox: knowing when to use a torque wrench versus an impact driver.
conceptual_breakdown: Factory vs Abstract Factory: Factory creates 1 product family; Abstract Factory creates families of related products (e.g. DarkTheme Button + Checkbox).
Strategy vs State: Strategy is chosen by client to vary an algorithm; State transitions automatically internally based on object state.
Decorator vs Adapter: Decorator adds behavior without changing interface; Adapter converts an incompatible interface into another.
Proxy vs Decorator: Proxy controls access (caching, security, lazy loading); Decorator enhances functionality.

steps.description: Need to add responsibilities to an object dynamically without subclassing? -> Use DECORATOR.
Need to match an incompatible legacy interface to a new client? -> Use ADAPTER.
Need to control lazy loading or permissions to an expensive object? -> Use PROXY.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Client-Driven Polymorphism: Strategy lets the caller dynamically swap algorithms at runtime.
2. Zero Code Duplication: Eliminates nested switch statements for format types.
3. Open for New Algorithms: Adding TarGzCompression requires zero edits to CompressionContext.

comparison_matrix.title: Pattern Nuances Comparison
rows: Adapter wraps 1 class to fix interface; Facade simplifies a whole subsystem
Adapter matches target interface; Facade creates new simple interface
Decorator adds new behavior; Proxy controls access/lifecycle
Both preserve the original interface identical to target
Observer is 1-to-many broadcast; Mediator encapsulates complex many-to-many communications
Mediator centralizes coordination; Observer distributes notifications

common_mistakes.mistake: Overusing Singleton for things that are not genuinely unique (e.g. User, Configuration)
common_mistakes.correction: Singleton creates hidden global state; prefer Dependency Injection.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why is the Visitor Pattern difficult to maintain if you frequently add new ConcreteElement classes?'
Answer: Adding a new element requires modifying the `IVisitor` interface and EVERY concrete visitor class, violating the Open-Closed Principle for the element dimension.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a hardcoded switch statement selecting sorting algorithms into the Strategy Pattern.

practice_problem.title: Select the Right Pattern for a Banking Pipeline
practice_problem.description: Which patterns would you use to design a Transaction processing pipeline with fraud scoring, fee calculation, ledger recording, and SMS alerts?
practice_problem.hint: Chain of Responsibility (pipeline) + Strategy (fee) + Observer (SMS alert).

topics.title: Concurrency & Multi-threading LLD Questions
topics.definition: Advanced questions on deadlocks, race conditions, memory models, reader-writer locking, double-checked locking, and thread pool starvation in C++.
topics.why_it_matters: Multi-threading is the ultimate filter in senior C++ LLD interviews. Demonstrating precise locking disciplines and lock-free awareness is essential.
topics.real_world_analogy: A 4-way traffic intersection: without traffic lights (locks) or roundabouts (lock-free), cars crash (data races) or create gridlock where nobody moves (deadlock).
conceptual_breakdown: 4 Conditions for Deadlock (Coffman): Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.
std::scoped_lock (C++17): Acquires multiple mutexes simultaneously using deadlock-avoidance algorithms (std::lock).
Thread-Safe Meyer's Singleton: Guaranteed thread-safe in C++11 with zero locking overhead after initialization.
False Sharing: Two threads writing to distinct variables on the same 64-byte cache line destroying performance.

steps.description: Thread 1 wants to transfer from Account A to Account B.
Thread 2 wants to transfer from Account B to Account A simultaneously.
Both use `std::scoped_lock(mtxA, mtxB)`. Deadlock avoidance algorithm acquires both without circular wait.
Transfers complete safely with zero deadlock risk!

step_by_step_explanation: 1. std::scoped_lock Deadlock Immunity: Eliminates lock-ordering bugs by acquiring all mutexes using a deadlock-avoidance algorithm.
2. Self-Transfer Guard: &from == &to check prevents trying to lock the same non-recursive mutex twice.
3. RAII Automatic Unlock: Mutexes are guaranteed unlocked upon function exit or exception throw.

common_mistakes.mistake: Acquiring mutexes in random order across different threads
common_mistakes.correction: Always use `std::scoped_lock` or enforce a global hierarchical acquisition order based on object memory addresses.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Is Double-Checked Locking safe in C++?'
Answer: In legacy C++98, it was broken due to CPU instruction reordering. In modern C++11+, Meyer's Singleton (`static Instance inst; return inst;`) is guaranteed thread-safe by the standard and should always be preferred over manual double-checked locking.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Fix a deadlock bug in an account transfer function acquiring locks sequentially.

practice_problem.title: Design Read-Write Thread-Safe Cache
practice_problem.description: Implement a key-value store using `std::shared_mutex` allowing unlimited concurrent readers but exclusive single-thread writers.

topics.title: Top 20 Critical C++ Interview Traps
topics.definition: The definitive compilation of subtle C++ traps, undefined behaviors, and design anti-patterns that frequently catch candidates off-guard in technical rounds.
topics.why_it_matters: Knowing these traps prevents unforced errors that lead to immediate disqualification by senior interviewers.
topics.real_world_analogy: A pilot's pre-flight checklist: checking pitot tubes, fuel contamination, and rudder locks before takeoff to eliminate fatal surprises.
conceptual_breakdown: Trap 1: Returning references/views to temporary local variables (Dangling References).
Trap 2: Iterator Invalidation when mutating vectors inside loops.
Trap 3: Slicing polymorphic objects by passing them by value.
Trap 4: Memory order relaxed races in custom lock-free queues.
Trap 5: Throwing exceptions from destructors (triggers `std::terminate`).

classes.name: Vector_Reallocation_Trap
attributes: push_back triggers reallocation to new heap address
Old iterators still point to freed memory -> CRASH!

steps.description: Vector capacity is full (4/4 elements at 0x1000).
push_back allocates new 8-element block at 0x5000 and frees 0x1000.
Dereferencing old iterator reads deallocated memory (Undefined Behavior / Crash).

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Dangling View Prevention: Never return std::string_view or std::span pointing to local stack variables.
2. Safe Container Modification: In C++20, use std::erase_if(vec, predicate) instead of manually calling vec.erase(it) inside a raw loop.
3. Lifetime Vigilance: Always track the lifetime owner of heap buffers when using non-owning pointer views.

comparison_matrix.title: Top 5 Critical Interview Pitfalls
rows: Store in `std::string` or ensure owner outlives view
`explicit Box(int size);` to prevent accidental casts

common_mistakes.correction: Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` to prevent unintended implicit type conversions.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Can a smart pointer circular reference occur with `std::unique_ptr`?'
Answer: No. `std::unique_ptr` enforces strict single exclusive ownership. Circular ownership cycles can only happen with `std::shared_ptr`, and are resolved using `std::weak_ptr`.
